newsitem.title: INDIA: Burning bodies litter India air crash site.
newsitem.headline: Burning bodies litter India air crash site.

text.p: Scores of bodies, some of them women and children, lay burning in fields amid the scattered remnants of two airplanes after the world's worst mid-air collision, witnesses were quoted as saying.

Thousands of horrified villagers watched as Indian rescue workers battled flames in an effort to retrieve corpses from the wreckage spread over a six-km (3.75-mile) radius some 80 km (50 miles) from New Delhi, the Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency reported.
"About 200 bodies, most of them burning, were sighted at the spot where relief and salvage operations were being hampered due to darkness," PTI said.
"The bodies of a number of victims, including women and children, were sighted burning in the fields," it added.
Around 350 people were feared killed when a Saudi Arabian jumbo jet taking off from New Delhi slammed into a descending Kazakh airliner around nightfall on Tuesday.
More than 20,000 villagers crowded round the crash site, where burning wreckage had gouged out a crater about 10 feet (three metres) deep, PTI said.
Three rescue teams, including more than 300 policemen, had cordoned off the wooded area, which lies in a sparsely-populated part of Haryana State.
Officials said there was little hope of finding survivors.
PTI said the Saudi jumbo jet "somersaulted thrice before the debris of the plane fell in the jungle area."
"The body of the pilot and one air hostess of the Saudi Airlines have been identified from their uniforms," PTI said.
Aviation officials said the flaming debris fell to earth near the village of Charkhi Dadri.
PTI quoted an eyewitness as saying: "I saw a ball of flame hurtling down and I could make out that it was an aircraft."
One aviation source said the collision was "like a bolt of lightning and two streaks of fire descended down to the ground."
"God only knows if there are any survivors," Robey Lal, an airport operations official at New Delhi airport, told Reuters.
A U.S. Air Force pilot flying nearby saw "two fireballs" plunge from the sky from the impact just at nightfall some 15,000 feet above northern India.

"In the distance off our right-hand side, two fireballs seemed to appear ... diverging away from each other," the pilot, who was bringing a military cargo plane into New Delhi, told reporters in Washington by telephone.
"The two fireballs proceeded to descend down and hit the ground and became fireballs on the ground," he said.
The Indian Air Force planned helicopter flights over the area at first light on Wednesday, civil aviation official Yogesh Chandra said.
Officials said there were 312 people, including 23 crew, aboard the Saudi Arabian Airlines flight SV 763, a Boeing 747.
The plane was bound for Dhahran and Jeddah in Saudi Arabia. Most of the passengers were Indians and Nepalis.
The Kazakh Airlines flight KZA 1907, an Ilyushin Il-76 cargo plane, carried 28 passengers and 10 crew, according to transport officials in the Central Asian state.
It was flying from Chimkent in Kazakhstan to New Delhi but had been chartered by a company in neighbouring Kyrgyzstan and most of the passengers aboard were Kyrgyz.
